sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, match the columns, true/false or a short passage).

questions.q: Read the passage and answer: 'The nervous system and the endocrine system work together as a team to control and coordinate all our activities. Sometimes we may not even be aware of their role in our health and well-being, and in our response to an urgent or dangerous situation.' (a) Name the two systems that control and coordinate all our body activities. (b) Which of these is usually executed in response to a dangerous situation? (A) Feeling of hunger (B) Role of digestive juices (C) Picking up food with the fingers (D) Immediate removal of the hand from a hot object
questions.answer: (a) The nervous system and the endocrine (hormonal) system. (b) (D) Immediate removal of the hand from a hot object (a reflex action).

questions.q: Read the passage and answer: 'The brain is well protected within the bony cranium. It is further protected by three meninges — dura mater (outermost, tough), arachnoid (delicate middle layer) and pia mater (innermost, highly vascular).' (1) Name the innermost meninx. (2) What is the function of the fluid present between the meninges?
questions.answer: (1) Pia mater. (2) Cerebrospinal fluid acts as a cushion that protects the brain from shocks (and helps exchange of materials).

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: The central nervous system consists of the ________ and the ________.
Match: (1) Cerebellum (2) Medulla oblongata — (a) intelligence and memory (b) balance and coordination of muscles (c) heartbeat and breathing (d) reflexes below the neck
Write True (T) or False (F): (1) Reflex actions are controlled by the cerebrum. (2) Hormones are carried to their target organs by the blood.
questions.answer: (1) False — they are controlled by the spinal cord. (2) True

sections.title: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

questions.q: At a synapse the impulse is carried across the gap by —

sections.passage: When your hand accidentally touches a hot pan, you pull it away at once, even before you feel pain. Such quick, automatic responses are called reflex actions. The receptor in the skin sends an impulse along a sensory neuron to the spinal cord, where an association neuron passes it to a motor neuron, which makes the muscles of the arm contract. Messages from one neuron to the next cross a small gap called a synapse with the help of chemicals.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Define nerves. Differentiate between sensory nerves and motor nerves with examples.
questions.answer: A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibres (axons) enclosed in a sheath, which carries impulses. Sensory nerves carry impulses from sense organs to the brain or spinal cord (e.g. the optic nerve); motor nerves carry impulses from the brain or spinal cord to muscles or glands (e.g. nerves to the eye muscles).

questions.q: What is a reflex action? Give two examples.
questions.answer: A reflex action is a quick, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus, controlled by the spinal cord without the involvement of the brain. Examples: withdrawing the hand from a hot object; blinking or tears flowing when dust enters the eye.

questions.q: Differentiate between the cerebrum and the cerebellum.
questions.answer: The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain, with two hemispheres; it controls thinking, memory, intelligence and voluntary actions. The cerebellum is smaller, below the cerebrum; it maintains balance and coordinates muscular movements.

questions.q: What is a hormone? Name the hormone whose shortage causes diabetes.
questions.answer: A hormone is a chemical secreted by an endocrine gland directly into the blood, which carries it to a target organ elsewhere to produce a specific effect. Insulin (from the pancreas).

questions.q: Name the two parts of the autonomic nervous system and give one function of each.
questions.answer: Sympathetic — prepares the body for emergencies (faster heartbeat, dilated pupils). Parasympathetic — restores normal conditions (slows the heartbeat, promotes saliva and digestion).

questions.q: Why does injury to the medulla oblongata often result in death?
questions.answer: The medulla controls vital involuntary actions such as heartbeat and breathing; if it is injured these may stop.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Name the three types of neurons and write their functions.
questions.answer: (1) Sensory neurons carry impulses from receptors (sense organs) to the brain or spinal cord. (2) Motor neurons carry impulses from the brain or spinal cord to effectors (muscles or glands). (3) Association (connecting) neurons, in the brain and spinal cord, connect sensory and motor neurons.

questions.q: Write three functions of the spinal cord.
questions.answer: (1) It controls reflex actions of the body below the neck. (2) It conducts sensory impulses from the skin and muscles to the brain. (3) It conducts motor impulses from the brain to the muscles of the trunk and limbs.

questions.q: Draw the generalised structure of a neuron and label dendrites, cell body, axon and nucleus.
questions.answer: Diagram: a cell body (cyton) containing a nucleus, with short branched dendrites on one side; from the other side a long axon covered by a sheath with nodes of Ranvier, ending in branched axon terminals (bulbs). Labels: dendrites, cell body, nucleus, axon.

or.q: (a) Name the hormone released by the thyroid gland and its function. (b) Define hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism.
or.answer: (a) Thyroxine; it controls the rate of metabolism and is needed for growth and development. (b) Hyperthyroidism: the thyroid is overactive and makes more hormone than needed. Hypothyroidism: the thyroid is underactive and makes less hormone than needed (in children it can cause cretinism).

questions.q: Draw a diagram of a synapse and label the synaptic vesicle, synaptic cleft, synaptic bulb and mitochondrion.
questions.answer: Diagram: the swollen end (synaptic bulb) of one neuron's axon lies close to the dendrite of the next neuron, separated by a narrow gap, the synaptic cleft. Inside the bulb are small round synaptic vesicles containing neurotransmitter and a few mitochondria. When an impulse arrives the vesicles release neurotransmitter into the cleft, which starts an impulse in the next neuron.

questions.q: Draw an outline of the human body and show the position of the glands that secrete (i) testosterone (ii) insulin (iii) the hormone whose malfunction causes severely stunted physical and mental growth (iv) the hormone whose malfunction causes dwarfism.
questions.answer: (i) Testes — in the scrotum below the abdomen. (ii) Pancreas — in the abdomen below the stomach. (iii) Thyroid — in the neck (cretinism). (iv) Pituitary — at the base of the brain (growth hormone).

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Define spinal reflex. Draw a labelled diagram of it.
questions.answer: A spinal reflex is a quick, automatic response to a stimulus that is controlled by the spinal cord without involving the brain, e.g. withdrawing the hand from a hot object. Diagram (reflex arc): a receptor in the skin of the hand → sensory neuron entering the spinal cord through the dorsal root → association (relay) neuron in the grey matter → motor neuron leaving through the ventral root → effector muscle in the arm, which contracts and pulls the hand away. The spinal cord section shows inner grey matter and outer white matter.

questions.q: Draw a neat diagram of a nerve cell (neuron) and label the nucleus, axon, dendrites and node of Ranvier. Give a brief description of the nerve cell.
questions.answer: Diagram: cell body with nucleus, short branched dendrites, a long axon with a fatty sheath interrupted at nodes of Ranvier, ending in terminal branches. Description: the neuron is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. Dendrites receive impulses and pass them to the cell body; the axon carries the impulse away; at its end, neurotransmitters released at a synapse pass the impulse to the next neuron or to a muscle or gland. The sheath insulates the axon, and the nodes of Ranvier help in fast transmission.

questions.q: Draw a sectional view of the human brain and label the part (i) whose infection causes meningitis (ii) which controls the beating of the heart (iii) which coordinates muscular movements (iv) which helps us memorise facts.
questions.answer: (i) Meninges — the three membranes (dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater) covering the brain. (ii) Medulla oblongata — at the base of the brain, continuing into the spinal cord. (iii) Cerebellum — below the back of the cerebrum. (iv) Cerebrum — the large upper part with two folded hemispheres.

questions.q: With the help of a labelled diagram, describe the internal structure of the spinal cord. State its functions.
questions.answer: In cross-section the spinal cord has an inner butterfly-shaped grey matter (cell bodies of neurons) surrounded by outer white matter (nerve fibres running to and from the brain), with a central canal filled with cerebrospinal fluid; it is covered by the dura mater, arachnoid and pia mater and lies in the neural canal of the backbone. Spinal nerves leave it through dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) roots. Functions: controls reflexes below the neck; carries sensory impulses to the brain; carries motor impulses from the brain to the trunk and limbs.
